html:
The philosophical traditions of Greece did not emerge from nothing. For millennia before Alcmaeon, physicians in Egypt, diagnosticians in Mesopotamia, and sages in Vedic India grappled with the organ of thought, the nature of awareness, and the reliability of perception. Their answers—sometimes startlingly empirical, sometimes embedded in cosmology and ritual—established many of the terms of debate that Greek philosophy would inherit and transform.

The Edwin Smith Papyrus

The Edwin Smith Papyrus (c. 1600 BCE, likely transcribed from a source dating to c. 2500 BCE) is the earliest known document to describe the brain—and contains the first recorded use of a word for “brain” in any surviving language 1. Across forty-eight case studies of traumatic injuries, organized systematically from head to spine, the anonymous Egyptian physician documented the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, and cranial sutures, and noted that injuries to the brain produce symptoms in distant parts of the body, including contralateral motor and sensory deficits. Each case is classified with remarkable clinical discipline as “an ailment I will treat,” “an ailment I will contend with,” or “an ailment not to be treated.” The papyrus represents a strikingly naturalistic, empirical approach to the brain as the organ that governs bodily experience—an approach that, as we shall see, was not shared by its own broader culture. The Egyptian Cardiac Doctrine

Despite the clinical insights of their physicians, Egyptian civilization as a whole located the mind not in the brain but in the heart (ib) 2, 3. The heart was the seat of intelligence, memory, emotion, and moral character—so central to personal identity that mummification practices carefully preserved it while the brain was extracted through the nostrils with hooks and discarded. In the weighing-of-the-heart scene depicted in the Book of the Dead, the deceased’s heart is placed on a scale against the feather of Ma’at (truth and cosmic order); if the heart is heavy with wrongdoing, the soul is devoured. The dominance of cardiac doctrine in a culture that simultaneously produced the Edwin Smith Papyrus’s brain observations is instructive for world-modeling theories: it demonstrates how powerfully prior beliefs—the generative model of a culture—can resist updating in the face of disconfirming evidence.

Esagil-kin-apli and the Mesopotamian Diagnostic Tradition

In Mesopotamia, the physician Esagil-kin-apli (c. 11th century BCE) compiled the Sakikkû (Diagnostic Handbook), the most systematic ancient compendium of disease classification prior to Hippocrates [Sakikkû]. Its forty tablets catalog neurological and psychiatric symptoms—seizures, paralysis, speech disturbances, altered states of consciousness, and what appear to be descriptions of stroke—organized by affected body region. However, unlike the Egyptian surgical tradition, the Sakikkû’s explanatory framework was overwhelmingly supernatural: symptoms were attributed to the actions of specific deities or demons. The Mesopotamian tradition thus embodies a paradox relevant to the philosophy of scientific modeling: meticulous empirical observation can coexist with a causal framework that, by modern lights, entirely misidentifies the generative process.

Yajnavalkya

The sage Yājnavalkya (c. 8th–7th century BCE), whose dialogues form the philosophical core of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad 4, produced what may be the earliest sustained analysis of consciousness as such. In his account of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, dreaming is especially revelatory: the mind, cut off from external sensation, “takes along the material of this all-encompassing world” and “tears it apart and builds it up again” from its own light. In deep dreamless sleep even this self-generated world dissolves, yet the self (Ātman) persists as pure awareness. For Yājnavalkya, the dream state demonstrates that the mind is fundamentally a world-generating system; the external environment merely constrains a process that would otherwise produce experience spontaneously—an insight whose resonance with the predictive processing view of perception as “controlled hallucination” is difficult to miss.

Uddalaka Aruni

Uddālaka Āruṇi (c. 8th–7th century BCE), the central teacher of the Chāndogya Upanishad 5, approached consciousness from a more naturalistic direction. In a celebrated passage, he instructs his son Śvetaketu that the mind depends on material nourishment: fast for fifteen days and thought degrades; eat again and it recovers. The mind (manas), on Uddālaka’s account, is composed of the subtlest portion of food—a substance-based theory of cognition that grounds mental life in metabolism. His teaching culminates in the mahāvākya “tat tvam asi” (“thou art that”): the deepest self and the fundamental reality of the world are identical. Where Yājnavalkya emphasized the self-generating autonomy of consciousness, Uddālaka emphasized its material dependence—a tension between internalist and externalist accounts of mind that persists in contemporary debates between predictive processing and enactivism.

Ptahhotep

Ptahhotep (c. 2400 BCE), vizier to the pharaoh Djedkare Isesi, composed the oldest surviving work of philosophical instruction 6. His thirty-seven maxims elaborate a cognitive psychology centered on the heart (ib): the heart is the organ of knowledge, judgment, intention, and moral reasoning, and its proper functioning determines the quality of a life. The cardinal intellectual virtue is sedjem—conventionally translated as “hearing” but denoting something closer to receptive, evaluative comprehension. The fool is defined not by ignorance but by a heart that “does not hear”: it receives sensory and social information but fails to integrate it correctly. The wise person’s heart hears, weighs, and responds with calibrated precision. For a world-modeling framework, Ptahhotep’s insistence that the same organ can receive identical input yet produce wise or foolish output—depending on the quality of its internal processing—is an early, if implicit, recognition that cognition is determined less by the data than by the model that interprets it.

The Nasadiya Sukta

The Nāsadīya Sūkta (Rig Veda X.129, c. 1200–1000 BCE), the celebrated Hymn of Creation, is among the most philosophically radical texts of the ancient world 7. “Then there was neither being nor non-being … Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an indistinguishable sea.” From this undifferentiated void, the hymn declares, kāma (desire, or primordial intentionality) arose as “the first seed of mind.” Desire—a directedness toward something not yet actual—is placed metaphysically prior to both the world and the consciousness that knows it. The hymn ends in radical epistemic humility: perhaps even the gods do not know how creation came about. For the philosophy of world modeling, the Nāsadīya Sūkta poses a question that modern enactivism inherits: does the world give rise to the mind that models it, or does something like mind (intentionality, directedness, the capacity for modeling) precede and condition the world?

Kapila and Early Samkhya

Kapila (traditionally c. 7th century BCE, though dating remains deeply uncertain) is credited as the founder of Sāṁkhya, one of the oldest systematic philosophies of mind and matter 8, 9. Sāṁkhya draws a sharp ontological line between puruṣa (pure consciousness—passive, unchanging, contentless awareness) and prakṛti (material nature—active, evolving, and encompassing not only the physical world but also the mind, senses, intellect, and ego). Cognition, perception, and every form of information processing belong entirely to prakṛti; puruṣa merely witnesses. This may be the oldest systematic mind–body dualism, but it inverts the Cartesian version: here it is consciousness, not matter, that is inert, and it is matter, not mind, that thinks. For computational neuroscience, Sāṁkhya sharpens a question that remains unresolved: is consciousness identical with information processing (as functionalism holds), or is it something that merely accompanies it—a witness to the computation rather than the computation itself?

Zarathustra

Zarathustra (Zoroaster; c. 1000–600 BCE, dating highly uncertain) articulated a cosmic and cognitive dualism in the Gāthās, the oldest stratum of the Avesta [Gāthās]. Reality is structured by the opposition between aša (truth, order, the way things are) and druj (falsehood, disorder, the way things are not), and the human mind is the arena in which this opposition plays out. Central to Zarathustra’s teaching is vohu manah (“good mind” or “right thinking”)—a cognitive and moral capacity to perceive and align with the true structure of reality. The human task is the exercise of vohu manah: discriminating truth from falsehood, real pattern from deceptive appearance, signal from noise. Embedded in cosmological and ethical language is what amounts to a proto-epistemological program: the mind’s fundamental operation is the separation of veridical models (those aligned with aša) from misspecified ones (those corrupted by druj)—a framing that resonates, at a considerable distance, with the Bayesian imperative to maintain accurate generative models of the world’s causal structure.
references: later codified in Īśvarakrṣṇa’s Sāṁkhya Kārikā
